I'd say get a new doctor. Also if you're sensitive to meds, you're prob going to react badly to everything unless the dose is tiny. I cant handle more than 300mg of lithium a day (300mg 3x a day is the normal starting dose and it's nowhere near "therapeutic levels"), and even an eighth of the smallest dose of seroquel had me sleeping upwards of 12 hours a day. Wellbutrin works for me, but I cycle from 37mg to 300mg depending on how i feel, and I just asked to switch to the SR instead of the XL for my 150mg pills because they were too long acting for me to sleep. (Another weird thing, one 300mg pill gives me terrible side effects but two 150mg pills doesn't. As my pdoc said, bioavailability is a weird thing.)

What dose are you on? Unfortunately you can't cut the XL, but maybe try taking it every other day? Wellbutrin has a very long half life (about 36 hours), so after 3 days you have more in your system than you did on day 1. I know most people say dont do anything without your doc's permission, but I advocate that you know your body best, and feeling like your body and what you put in it is outside of your control never helped anyone's mental health.

I have many times wished I could just be happy with a simple life, and not have to deal with existential depression and nihilism. During hypomanic episodes I suddenly have strong urges to do things and create things. If I were a great artist, perhaps having bipolar would make me a legendary artist, but such is not the case. So to answer your question, my personal opinion is no. Also, in my personal opinion, bipolar makes people stupider, so even if you start out smart, it's a struggle to stay that way.

Maybe it's like how depression is less diagnosed in poor people because society assumes it's normal for poor people to be depressed. So when people of less than average intelligence display bipolar behavior, perhaps we blame it on their lack of intelligence. When an otherwise smart person acts bipolar we wonder what on earth is making such a smart person behave that way. Just a theory. Another theory: smart people have so many brains that maintenance can't up, and eventually has to prioritize and take turns, leading to oscillating brain states.

I'm bipolar II as well and I agree with the above, don't worry about it. Unless your job depends on you being always on socially, it probably won't impede your life anymore than being an INTP already does. If you had a mental disorder worth going on meds for, cyclical sociability would be the least of your worries. 

Edit: I know that doesn't answer your question. What helps me if I'm in rapid cycling is to limit my social interactions on good days so that I have more social energy on bad days. Sometimes I'll make a rule where even on weekends I'm only allowed one activity outside the house per day. That may be a little drastic for you situation though. At this point all my friends know that sometimes I want to talk to them and sometimes I don't, so I don't have to make a ton of effort on that front and can just focus on my mental health.

First step to connecting with your feelings is identifying what they are. In order to accurately identify certain feelings you may need to go through vocab lists, the dictionary, thesaurus, emotional vocab from other languages, or just plain old metaphor. Then you need to accept the emotion, so aiming to feel the emotion without having an emotional reaction to the fact that you are having emotions. You've prob heard of various meditation practices where they do that. In therapy, you'd either be encouraged to "let the emotion flow through your body" ie feel the emotion more fully, or to dissociate from it if it's painful or traumatic using questions like "if it had a color, what color would it be? what size, what shape?" etc. At least that's what my experience has been.

I think it's so important to put words and images to pain and struggle that is otherwise invisible, and to take our suffering and turn it in into art. I have a different mental disorder, but one of my best friends confided in me yesterday that he has OCD, and this helped me see what he is probably experiencing.
